charts.title: Cash vs Total Debt vs Net Financial Debt

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Legrand SA: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash, debt and net financial debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted). Net financial debt is Legrand's own disclosed leverage metric, not simply Total debt minus Cash -- it reflects the company's own scope for financial liabilities and can diverge from a generic bridge, e.g. around the June 2025 OCEANE convertible (EUR 800m face), which Legrand carries as debt but whose equity component and redemption premium are treated separately in the DCF's bridge.

For Legrand SA: net financial debt rose from roughly EUR 2.0bn (FY2024) to EUR 4.2bn (FY2025), largely the OCEANE issuance; the DCF's net-debt bridge works from the balance-sheet total debt and cash, so compare the two leverage views rather than assuming they are interchangeable.

What to watch:

  • Net financial debt trend versus EBITDA
  • The OCEANE's conversion price (EUR 159.03) versus the share price -- equity conversion versus a 2033 cash repayment
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Legrand SA: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Legrand SA: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Legrand SA: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Legrand SA: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Legrand SA: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Legrand SA: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs. Organic growth % is Legrand's own disclosed constant-scope, constant-currency growth rate -- it strips out acquisitions, disposals and FX translation, leaving only like-for-like volume and price.

For Legrand SA: Legrand has been a serial acquirer (EUR hundreds of millions per year of bolt-on M&A), so reported revenue growth routinely runs well above organic growth; the gap between the two lines is the contribution from deals and currency, not the underlying business. Organic growth also uncovers soft patches reported growth can mask, e.g. +2.7% and +1.0% organic in FY2023-24 during the building-market slowdown.

What to watch:

  • Reported growth persistently above organic growth (M&A-fuelled, not organic, expansion)
  • Organic growth decelerating even if reported growth looks fine
  • Organic growth is FY-only as disclosed; interim figures are not restated here

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Legrand SA: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
